ideas.title: Release-contract linter for npm packages
ideas.summary: Before publishing, check the parts of a release's contract that type checkers ignore: engine requirements tightened, entry points or exports paths removed, module format switched, new required peer dependencies, removed CLI commands. Fail if a minor or patch release changes them.
ideas.targetUsers: Maintainers of JavaScript and TypeScript packages on npm (including packages without types)
ideas.solution: A CLI and GitHub Action that compares the package.json and published file list of the release candidate with the last published version on npm, and flags contract changes that need a major bump (engines.node raised, exports subpaths removed or an exports map added, main/module/types removed, type: module switch, new non-optional peer dependencies, bin entries removed). It can run alongside a type-surface checker.
ideas.differentiation: Existing tools inspect the TypeScript type surface. This inspects the install- and import-time contract, which breaks even for untyped packages (e.g. polished's engines bump). It complements the type checkers rather than replacing them.
ideas.feasibility: High. Everything needed is in package.json and the npm registry metadata. No compiler work is needed.

assumptions.text: Metadata-level contract breaks in minor or patch releases are common among popular packages (≥ 20% shipped at least one in two years)
Flags are mostly genuine breaks rather than noise (≥ 70% of audited flags)
Maintainers would add another check to their release workflow
The structural-only rule set (no engine-range rule) is precise on packages it wasn't tuned on (≥ 70% of audited flags genuine)

risks: The rules may be too strict (some engines bumps are deliberate and announced)
Existing checkers may add metadata rules
nextSteps: If supported, build the CLI and dogfood it on real packages

objections.text: Behaviour changes, like React 16.4's, are invisible to any static check, so this catches only part of the problem.
objections.response: It doesn't need to catch everything to be useful. The experiment measures how much it catches.

objections.text: Some maintainers deliberately tighten engines in minor releases (e.g. dropping end-of-life Node). They may consider that acceptable, and see the linter as noise.
objections.response: The audit step measures how many flags are genuine. Rules can be configured.

objections.text: The type-checker projects could add metadata rules quickly.
Engine-range rules dominate the flags and are mostly debatable (dropping end-of-life Node), which made 60% of audited flags non-genuine.
objections.response: A narrowed, structural-only rule set was 78% precise in the audit (exploratory), but fires for only about 10% of popular packages.

severity.rationale: Breaking minor releases cost users real time.

frequency.rationale: Frequency of metadata breaks unknown; being measured.

userValue.rationale: Catches a class of breaks no current tool checks, before publish.

competitiveGap.rationale: No tool found that checks the install/import contract.

userAccess.rationale: Maintainers reachable via GitHub Marketplace and npm.

validationCost.rationale: Frequency testable for $0 on registry data.

ideas.statusRationale: Parked with a narrowed recommendation. As specified, the linter is too noisy (40% genuine). A structural-only rule set looks precise (about 78% in a small exploratory sample) but helps only about 1 in 10 popular packages. Its practical value is as a 'compare with last release' feature for an existing linter like publint, pending validation on a fresh sample.
ideas.noveltyNote: Distinct from the rejected type-surface checker: it inspects package metadata and the published file contract, not .d.ts types.

practical.adopters: npm package maintainers, as a pre-publish check, and possibly downstream teams auditing updates
practical.smallestUsefulVersion: A 'compare with last release' mode for publint (or a small plugin) with the structural rules: removed export paths, entry fields, CLI commands and peer tightening. Engine checks only if they know Node's end-of-life dates.
practical.buildNote: Needs only package.json parsing, npm registry metadata and the semver library. VENTURE already uses all three.
practical.monetization: None realistic: best as an upstream contribution to existing open-source linters.

experiments.title: Do structural release-contract rules stay precise on fresh packages?
experiments.hypothesis: On 400 popular npm packages not in the first study, structural rules alone flag at least one minor or patch release in at least 5% of packages over 24 months, and at least 70% of 20 audited flags are genuine breaking changes.
experiments.uncertainty: The structural rules' 7-of-9 precision came from a post-hoc subset of the first audit, dominated by a few release trains. This tests it on packages and flags the rules were not tuned on (assumption a4).
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-16 before any data for the new population was collected.
Population: npm search, keywords vue, eslint, test, css, database, http (250 each, ranked by popularity), excluding all 400 packages of exp-npm-metadata-breaks; first 400 unique names.
Release pairs: identical to exp-npm-metadata-breaks (consecutive non-prerelease minor or patch releases within a major line ≥ 1, published 2024-11-04 to 2026-11-04).

Rules: the structural rules of exp-npm-metadata-breaks unchanged (exports subpath removed or exports map added, main/module/types/typings removed, switch to type module, new required peer or a peer's minimum major raised, bin removed). The engines rule is excluded.

Audit: 20 flags drawn by fixed seed 'venture-structural-2026-11-16', at most one per package family (npm scope, or name when unscoped). Judged by a research session with the criteria of the first audit, unchanged: genuine, debatable, or not genuine.
successCriteria: At least 5% of packages have a structural flag, and at least 14 of the 20 audited flags (70%) are genuine
failureCriteria: Fewer than 5% of packages have a structural flag (too rare to be worth a feature)
Fewer than 10 of the 20 audited flags (50%) are genuine (too noisy)
experiments.estimatedTime: < 1 hour of automated analysis plus a manual audit of 20 flags
experiments.expectedLearning: Whether the narrowed rule set is precise enough to propose upstream, judged on data it was not derived from.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Prototype a 'compare with last release' check and ask the owner whether VENTURE may propose it to publint's maintainers.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Reject the idea: even the narrowed rule set is not reliable enough to recommend.

decisions.rationale: Still parked. Added assumption a4 (the structural-only rules are precise on fresh packages) and pre-registered exp-npm-structural-breaks to test it before any upstream proposal.

briefs.researchQuestion: Libraries regularly ship 'minor' or 'patch' updates that break the code of everyone using them, even though those updates are installed automatically on the promise of being safe. Could a small open-source tool catch these breaks before a release is published?
briefs.whyItMatters: Every JavaScript project depends on dozens to hundreds of packages and trusts version numbers to signal risk. When a minor release breaks that trust, users lose time pinning versions and debugging, and maintainers lose credibility. Rust has a widely adopted tool for this; JavaScript has no established equivalent.
subQuestions: How often do popular npm packages ship breaking changes in minor or patch releases?
What kinds of breaks are they: type changes, behaviour changes, or metadata changes?
What do existing and emerging tools catch, and what do they miss?
Is there a small, buildable tool that catches a meaningful share with little noise?

findings.statement: Breaking minor and patch releases cost users real time. Reports describe whole codebases breaking after a React minor update, release pipelines broken for a weekend, and maintainers forced to pin versions. Microsoft built API Extractor partly because users 'keep reporting that their code won't compile after a supposedly minor update'.
findings.strength: Moderate. Several independent reports plus Microsoft's own stated motivation. Individual cases, not a measured rate.

findings.statement: The tool model works elsewhere: Rust's cargo-semver-checks (about 1,700 stars, with a GitHub Action) checks releases for semver violations, though it documents breaks it can't catch.
findings.strength: Strong as evidence that a tool exists and is adopted in Rust. It doesn't show JS maintainers would adopt one.

findings.statement: The TypeScript type-surface checker niche is filling up: Clerk's break-check (company-backed), ts-semver-checks and semver-check all appeared in 2026, alongside Microsoft's API Extractor.
findings.strength: Strong for existence. All are very new, with little adoption yet.

findings.statement: Type checkers miss many real breaks. None of the four complaints examined was a type change: they were behaviour changes (React, floating-ui, node-abort-controller) and a metadata change (polished raised its required Node version in a minor release).
findings.strength: Weak to moderate. A small sample, but it points to a clear gap: the install and import contract in package metadata.

findings.statement: Metadata-level contract breaks are common: by the linter's rules, 20% of 400 popular npm packages shipped at least one in a minor or patch release over two years. But as specified the rules are too noisy: only 8 of 20 audited flags were genuine breaks. Most of the rest were debatable engine-range changes dropping end-of-life Node versions.
findings.strength: Moderate. A pre-registered measurement plus a hand audit of 20 flags against criteria fixed beforehand (one reviewer).

findings.statement: The structural rules are the useful core. Removed export paths, entry fields and CLI commands, and tightened peers, were genuine in 7 of 9 audited cases, but they fire for only about 10% of popular packages over two years. Many flags come from a few fast-moving projects (@tanstack, better-auth, @typescript-eslint).
findings.strength: Weak to moderate. Exploratory, post hoc, small n.

uncertainties: Whether the structural-only rules stay precise on packages they weren't tuned on (being measured).
Whether maintainers consider deliberate engine bumps in minor releases acceptable.
The four complaints were chosen by GitHub search ranking, not sampled randomly.

conclusion.belief: Accidental breaking releases are real, and a cheap metadata check can catch a share of them that type checkers miss: removed export paths, entry points and CLI commands, and tightened peers. But it's a modest benefit (about 1 in 10 popular packages over two years). As first specified, engine-range rules make it too noisy. The practical value is a small, precise rule set, best contributed as a 'compare with last release' mode to an existing packaging linter such as publint. That would be useful open-source work, but not a standalone product.
conclusion.confidenceReason: A pre-registered measurement over 12,240 release pairs plus an audited sample. Not high: the audit had one reviewer and 20 flags, and the narrowed rule set's precision comes from only 9 audited cases.
unknowns: The narrowed rule set's precision on a fresh sample
Whether publint's maintainers would want this feature
How often flagged breaks actually hurt users (issues filed after release)
conclusion.continueReason: One cheap step remains: validate the narrowed rule set on a fresh, independently drawn audit sample before proposing it upstream.

nextSteps.text: Replicate the structural-only rule set on 400 fresh popular packages, auditing 20 flags with at most one per package family (pre-registered: ≥ 5% of packages flagged and ≥ 70% genuine).
If it holds, prototype a 'compare with last release' check, and ask the owner whether VENTURE may propose it to the publint maintainers. That means contacting people, so it needs authorization.
